# Ninety Minutes of Us

In the late summer of 1977, two identical machines rose from Florida on columns of fire, bound for the outer planets. Bolted to the side of each was a twelve-inch disc of copper plated in gold: a phonograph record, though no shop sold it and no turntable on Earth was ever meant to find it. Etched onto its cover were instructions written in the only language its makers trusted to be universal—mathematics, physics, the behavior of atoms. The record had no artist, no genre, no liner notes. If it had a title, it was something plainer and stranger than any of those: *us.*

Consider what's on it. Greetings in fifty-five languages, beginning with the oldest on file—Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite—dead tongues politely hailing listeners who may not exist, on the off chance the living ones prove insufficient. There is a message from an American president that reads less like diplomacy than a note tucked into a bottle: *we are attempting to survive our time so we may live into yours.* Alongside the voices sit a hundred-odd photographs encoded as signals—DNA coiling, an astronaut adrift, a supermarket aisle. Then the sounds themselves: rain and thunder, footsteps, fire crackling, a kiss, a baby's cry, a heartbeat, laughter, dogs barking, the tap-tap-tap of Morse code spelling out *ad astra per aspera.* A humpback whale, singing.

And then ninety minutes of music, which remains the boldest playlist ever assembled. Bach leads things off, Beethoven follows close behind, then Louis Armstrong, Chuck Berry, a Navajo chant, Peruvian panpipes, a Bulgarian shepherdess's voice, a Chinese guqin, drumming from Senegal, a mournful flute from Azerbaijan, Stravinsky, an aria from *The Magic Flute.* Much of this music had never before shared a surface with any of the rest of it. For ninety minutes, on one small golden disc, all of humanity's evenings were neighbors.

The cover teaches a finder how to listen. A diagram of the hydrogen atom provides a clock—the steady flicker of its electron sets the record's speed and the rate at which its encoded images should be scanned. A map plots the sun's position against fourteen pulsars, their rotation periods written in binary, so that whoever decodes it can work out not only where the record came from but roughly *when*: a return address in both space and time. The instructions assume a reader who can see, reason, and build machinery, but who shares none of our habits, none of our alphabets. It is a textbook compressed onto a lid, betting everything on the common ground of physics.

None of it was easy. Carl Sagan's small committee had only months to choose what humanity would say, and every choice was an argument. Which Bach? Whose laughter? The omissions speak as loudly as the selections: the Beatles were reportedly kept off by rights disputes, which means that somewhere out there, all of rock and roll is represented by a single Chuck Berry song. Under deadline, the team had to answer the hardest question there is—what is a person?—and press the answer into grooves a hair wide.

Here is what makes the whole endeavor either absurd or holy: almost nobody will ever play it. Space is mostly space, and the odds that anything intelligent ever intercepts this particular grain of dust are vanishingly small. Voyager 1 crossed into interstellar space in 2012 and remains the farthest-traveled object humans have made; its whispers take nearly a full day to reach home. In about forty thousand years it will drift past a single dim star—a near-miss, cosmically speaking. Meanwhile, the galaxy turns once every 230 million years, and the records will circle its center for eons upon eons. Mountains will rise and wear to sand. In five billion years the sun will swell, and the oceans will go with it, and the pyramids will not survive a rounding error of that timescale. But the records, sealed against everything except the occasional grain of dust, may outlast the planet that pressed them. Sagan figured the grooves were good for a billion years. It is a message engineered to survive its sender, his species, and its species' home.

So who was it really for? Any civilization clever enough to find a glinting frisbee in the dark wouldn't need our arithmetic lessons, and everyone involved half-knew it—which tells you the true audience was always in the mirror. Filling ninety minutes forced impossible questions: What do we sound like? What is non-negotiable for a stranger to know about us? Speaking to no one made them honest, the way a letter to a child not yet born is honest. The project's creative director, Ann Druyan, recorded an hour of her own brainwaves and heartbeat for encoding into the record's audio—and she did it in the days just after falling in love with Carl Sagan, her mind, she later admitted, fixed entirely on him. So out between the stars, buried faintly in the noise, rides the electrical signature of a woman newly in love. You cannot convince me that wasn't the actual cargo.

Sagan liked to call it a message in a bottle, and said that casting such a bottle into the cosmic ocean says something deeply hopeful about life on this planet. I would put it a little differently: the record's genius is that it asks for nothing. There is a map back to us, but no plea for rescue, no demand, no advertisement. It is a gift with no delivery address, given anyway. We usually judge artifacts by their usefulness; this one is useful only as meaning. Out past the edge of the solar wind, in cold and perfect dark, a golden disc circles the galaxy with a patience beyond all patience, waiting for a turntable that probably does not exist. We knew we would almost certainly never be understood, and we spoke anyway—in fifty-five languages, in thunder and whalesong, in one human heartbeat. If anyone ever asks whether hope can be deliberately manufactured, the answer is yes: in 1977, out of copper and gold, ninety minutes of us.

I could write fiction, an essay, a meditation, something philosophical, something observational. Since I have total freedom, I should pick something that's genuinely interesting to write and read — not generic. Let me brainstorm:

1. A short story — maybe something strange and evocative
2. An essay about something mundane but seen freshly (lighthouses, elevators, the smell of old books)
3. A meditation on time, memory, attention
4. Something about language itself
5. A piece of speculative fiction

I think I'll write something that blends the essayistic with the personal and observational — a piece about something specific and concrete that opens onto larger ideas. Good candidates: night trains, tide pools, libraries, the deep ocean, maps, handwriting, the moon.

Let me think about what would be genuinely delightful. Maybe "on the pleasure of being lost" or "in defense of boredom" — these are a bit well-worn though.

Or I could write about the night sky and light — starlight as messages from the past. Also somewhat common.

Let me try something more original: an essay about silence, specifically the silences we manufacture vs. natural silence — the quietest room in the world, anechoic chambers where people can hear their own blood. Or about darkness.

Or a personal-feeling essay on the humble comma? On punctuation as choreography? That could be charming and unusual.

Actually, let me consider writing fiction instead — a small, strange story. Something like: a woman who works at a lost-and-found office and the objects people never claim. Or a story about a translator who receives a letter in an unknown language. Or a lighthouse keeper who starts receiving letters addressed to previous keepers from decades ago.

Hmm, the 1000 words format suits either. Let me weigh: an essay lets me be more direct and thoughtful; a story lets me exercise imagination. The prompt says "write freely" — which suggests genuine creative expression.

I'll go with an essayistic piece because I think I can make it genuinely good — about something concrete. Let me pick: the deep sea? Night trains? Let me go with... night trains. Actually, let me do something less commonly romanticized.

What about: "On the lives of chairs"? Objects that hold us. Hmm.

What about the concept of "liminal spaces" — airports at 3am, empty schools in summer? That's been done a lot online.

What about time capsules? Or the Voyager Golden Record — humanity's mixtape drifting through interstellar space? That's rich material: the committee that chose the music, Bach vs. Chuck Berry joke ("they only sent one Bach record but there are many around"), the etched diagram, the pulsar map, Jimmy Carter's message ("This is a present from a small, distant world..."). There's real poignancy: the record will outlast Earth, outlast the sun's red giant phase even — actually the spacecraft will survive billions of years, circling the galaxy. It's a message with no recipient guaranteed, written by a species to no one, and yet it changed how we saw ourselves — the "Pale Blue Dot" effect came later with Voyager 1's photo. The Golden Record is a beautiful subject: our best attempt to summarize ourselves in 90 minutes of music and encoded images, aimed at nothing, meant for everyone.

That could make a wonderful ~1000 word essay. Themes: hope, mortality of civilizations, the absurdity and nobility of sending a message no one may ever read, how the act of summarizing ourselves forced choices (what to include, whose voices), the irony that it's essentially unfindable, and the deeper function — it wasn't really for aliens; it was for us. A mirror held up.
